title: Monolith vs Microservices & Service Architecture
summary: How you split a system into deployable pieces decides how fast teams ship and how badly it fails. Choose for your org, not the hype.

blocks.markdown:
It's a choice about **deployment boundaries**, not code quality.

- A **monolith** is one codebase that builds and deploys as a single process; modules call each other in-memory.
- **Microservices** split the system into many services, each deployed independently and talking over the network.
- A **modular monolith** is the middle: one deployable, but strict internal boundaries — clean separation without the network tax.
- The real driver is **independent deployability and team autonomy** — an organizational tool first, a technical one second.

blocks.subTitle: When to reach for each
blocks.markdown:
Default to a modular monolith; extract a service only under measured pressure.

| Situation | Reach for |
|---|---|
| New product, small team | Modular monolith |
| One part scales differently | Extract that one service |
| Many teams, one release train | Microservices by team |
| Tight cross-entity consistency | Keep in one service/DB |

blocks.subTitle: The split
blocks.markdown:
The split turns in-memory calls into network hops.

![Monolith versus microservices side by side](assets/b16-monolith-microservices/monolith-vs-microservices.svg)

- A monolith bundles Orders, Payments, Users, Inventory as modules over **one shared database**.
- Microservices give each capability its own process, deploy pipeline, and **private database**.
- More boxes *and* more arrows — every arrow is a place that can be slow or fail.
- Everything hard about microservices flows from this: function calls become network calls.

assets.alt: Monolith versus microservices side by side

blocks.subTitle: What a network hop costs
blocks.markdown:
An in-process call is nanoseconds and never half-fails; a network hop is neither.

- A same-datacenter RPC is ~**0.5–2 ms** — roughly 10,000–100,000× slower — and can time out, duplicate, or hang.
- A request fanning out to 5 services pays latency 5× and fails if **any** one is down.
- At 99.9% each, a chain of 5 is 0.999^5 ≈ **99.5%** — you got *worse* by adding services.
- This is why you avoid deep synchronous call chains.

blocks.subTitle: Bounded contexts
blocks.markdown:
Find boundaries where the **language** and **data ownership** naturally change.

- A **bounded context** is a slice where a word means one thing and data has one owner.
- "Customer" in billing (payment method, tax ID) differs from "Customer" in support (tickets, score).
- Cut where the ubiquitous language shifts; each context is a service candidate.
- **Smell test:** if one operation must read *and* write across the line in one breath, the line is wrong. See [d03-domain-driven-design](d03-domain-driven-design.md).

blocks.subTitle: Database-per-service
blocks.markdown:
The load-bearing rule: each service owns a **private** datastore no one else touches.

- If Orders needs a user's email, it calls the Users API or listens to an event — never queries the Users table.
- The moment two services share a table, neither can change its schema without coordinating both deploys.
- Private data is exactly what buys **independent deployability**.
- The cost: cross-service `JOIN`s and ACID transactions are gone — replaced by API composition, CQRS read models, and sagas.

blocks.subTitle: Sagas for cross-service transactions
blocks.markdown:
With no shared DB, a **saga** replaces the cross-service transaction.

![Place-order saga with compensation on failure](assets/b16-monolith-microservices/saga-database-per-service.svg)

- It's a sequence of local commits, each with a **compensating action** that semantically undoes it.
- On failure, run compensations backward — refund the payment, cancel the order. There is no distributed rollback.
- **Choreography**: services react to events, no central brain. **Orchestration**: a coordinator drives steps.
- A saga is **eventually consistent** — the UI must tolerate in-progress states.

assets.alt: Place-order saga with compensation on failure

blocks.subTitle: Service discovery
blocks.markdown:
Instances come and go, so addresses aren't stable — discovery finds healthy ones.

![Service discovery with sidecar proxies](assets/b16-monolith-microservices/service-discovery-sidecar.svg)

- A **service registry** (Consul, etcd, Kubernetes Endpoints) holds the live, health-checked list.
- Instances **register** and **heartbeat**; the registry drops unhealthy ones; callers **resolve** a name.
- A **sidecar / service mesh** (Envoy) handles discovery, load balancing, retries, timeouts, and mTLS.
- The app just calls `localhost` and stays ignorant of the network.

blocks.subTitle: What you actually trade
blocks.markdown:
Microservices swap an in-process problem for a distributed-systems one.

| You gain | You pay |
|---|---|
| Independent deploys | Operational complexity |
| Team autonomy | Cross-service debugging |
| Independent scaling | Eventual consistency, sagas |
| Failure isolation | More machines, network cost |

You need real platform investment (CI/CD, observability, mesh) before it pays off.

blocks.subTitle: Decision rules
blocks.markdown:
Plain-English defaults — extract only under measured pressure.

- **Small team, unproven domain** → modular monolith; you don't know the boundaries yet.
- **One part scales/fails differently** (CPU-bound media, flaky integration) → extract just that one.
- **Many teams on a shared release train** → split along team lines (Conway's Law).
- **Strong cross-entity consistency** → keep it in one service/DB; don't saga what a transaction can do.
- **Can't draw clean boundaries** → don't split; a wrong network boundary is far costlier to fix.

blocks.subTitle: Real systems
blocks.markdown:
The famous migrations — and a reversal — teach the trade.

- **Amazon** — a service-interface mandate, no shared DBs, birthing two-pizza teams and AWS-style SOA.
- **Netflix** — hundreds of services on AWS, backed by heavy platform tooling (discovery, circuit breakers, Chaos Monkey).
- **Segment** — split, hit a distributed monolith, then *consolidated back* to a monolith in 2018.
- **Shopify** — a disciplined **modular monolith** at scale, boundaries enforced by Packwerk.

blocks.subTitle: Conway's Law & migration
blocks.markdown:
Your architecture will mirror your org chart whether you plan it or not.

- **Conway's Law:** a system's design mirrors the communication structure of the org that builds it.
- Want N services? You generally need ~N teams that own them. The **Inverse Conway Maneuver** structures teams to get the architecture you want.
- Migrate with the **strangler fig**: route some traffic to a new service, migrate its data, cut over — never big-bang rewrite.
- Extract the highest-pain, most-independent context first.

The misconceptions that cause real pain:

- **"Microservices make code cleaner."** No — they move the mess across a network. Get good boundaries in a monolith first.
- **"We'll share a database, just for now."** That's the fastest way to a **distributed monolith**; the coupling becomes permanent.
- **"Sagas are just distributed transactions."** No rollback, only compensation, and a visible window of inconsistency.
- **"We need microservices to scale."** Usually you can scale a monolith horizontally far past where you are.
- **"Start with microservices to avoid migrating later."** Premature decomposition freezes boundaries you don't understand yet.
